q:
Arrange the following types of cohesion from best to worst:

- (A) Logical cohesion
- (B) Sequential cohesion
- (C) Communicational cohesion
- (D) Temporal cohesion
- (E) Procedural cohesion
exp: The standard cohesion scale from strongest to weakest is functional, sequential, communicational, procedural, temporal, logical, coincidental. Keeping only the five listed types gives sequential (B), communicational (C), procedural (E), temporal (D), logical (A).
trick: Mnemonic from worst to best: Coincidental, Logical, Temporal, Procedural, Communicational, Sequential, Functional — read it backwards for best-to-worst.

q:
To create an object-behavioral model, the analyst performs the following steps:

- (A) Evaluates all use-cases
- (B) Builds a state transition diagram for the system
- (C) Reviews the object behavior model to verify accuracy and consistency
- (D) Identifies events that do not drive the interaction sequence
exp: Behavioural modelling starts by evaluating all use cases to understand the interaction sequence, identifies the events that *do* drive that sequence, builds a state transition diagram, and finally reviews the model for accuracy and consistency. Step (D) is the odd one out because the analyst looks for events that drive the sequence, not ones that do not.
trick: In these Pressman step-list questions, the false step is usually a correct step with a negation slipped into it — read for "do not".

q: A software project was estimated at 864 function points. A six-person team will be assigned to the project consisting of one requirement-gathering person, one designer, two programmers and two testers. The salary of the designer is Rs 70,000 per month, the requirement gatherer Rs 50,000 per month, a programmer Rs 60,000 per month and a tester Rs 60,000 per month. The average productivity for the team is 12 FP per person-month. Which of the following represents the projected cost of the project?
exp: Effort $= 864 / 12 = 72$ person-months, and with six people that is $72/6 = 12$ calendar months. The team costs $50000 + 70000 + 2(60000) + 2(60000) = $ Rs 3,60,000 per month, so the total is $12 \times 360000 = $ Rs 43,20,000.
trick: Total cost = (FP / productivity) person-months, then multiply by the *average* monthly salary — or equivalently by team monthly cost over duration. Both routes give the same figure.

q: Which of the following UML diagrams has a static view?
exp: Collaboration (communication), state chart and activity diagrams all model how the system changes over time — messages in sequence, state transitions and control flow. A use-case diagram simply shows actors, use cases and their associations without any notion of ordering or time, so it presents a static view of system functionality.
trick: If a diagram has an ordering, a trigger or a transition, it is dynamic. Use-case and class diagrams have none, so they are the static ones.

q:
Software reliability is described with respect to

- (A) Execution time
- (B) Calendar time
- (C) Clock time
exp: Reliability models measure time in three different ways: execution (CPU) time actually spent running the program, calendar time as it elapses for the project, and clock/wall time that the system is powered and available. All three are legitimate time bases for stating a reliability or failure-intensity figure.

q: Software reuse is
opts: Process of analysing software for design/specification recovery
Process of using existing software artifacts to build new software
Analysing software for higher abstraction representation
exp: Reuse means building a new system out of already-existing artifacts (components, libraries, designs, patterns) instead of writing them again. The other three options describe reverse engineering, re-engineering and abstraction recovery respectively.
trick: Reuse = use old parts in new systems. Reverse engineering = recover design from code. Re-engineering = rebuild the old system itself.

q: Software validation checks for inconsistencies between
exp: Validation asks "are we building the right product?", i.e. it compares what was specified and built against what the customer actually wants. So it looks for mismatches between the specification and the user requirements. Verification, by contrast, compares the implementation against the design.
trick: Validation = against the *requirements* (right product). Verification = against the *design/specification* (product right).

q:
In the context of software testing, which of the following statements is/are NOT correct?

- P: A minimal test set that achieves 100% path coverage will also achieve 100% statement coverage.
- Q: A minimal test set that achieves 100% path coverage will generally detect more faults than one that achieves 100% statement coverage.
- R: A minimal test set that achieves 100% statement coverage will generally detect more faults than one that achieves 100% branch coverage.
exp: P is correct because every statement lies on some path, so full path coverage subsumes statement coverage. Q is correct because path coverage is the strongest of the three criteria. R is the wrong one: branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, so branch-covering tests generally find more faults, not fewer.
trick: Strength order: path $\supset$ branch $\supset$ statement. Any claim that a weaker criterion finds more faults is the false one.

q: A web application and its support environment have not been fully fortified against attack. The likelihood of repelling an attack is 30 percent. The application does not contain sensitive or controversial information, so the threat probability is 25 percent. What is the integrity of the web application?
exp: Integrity is computed as $1 - \sum (\text{threat} \times \text{failure to repel})$, where failure to repel is $1 - 0.30 = 0.70$. So integrity $= 1 - (0.25 \times 0.70) = 1 - 0.175 = 0.825$.
trick: Integrity $= 1 - \sum[\text{threat} \times (1-\text{security})]$ — the 30% is the security term, so multiply by 0.7, not 0.3.

q: An ______ chart is a project schedule representation that presents the project plan as a directed graph. The critical path is the ______ sequence of ______ tasks and it defines the project ______.
exp: An activity network (activity chart) draws tasks and their precedence as a directed graph. The critical path is the longest chain of mutually dependent tasks through that graph, and since no slack exists on it, its length is exactly the minimum project duration.
trick: Critical path = LONGEST path and therefore the SHORTEST possible project duration. Tasks on it are dependent and have zero slack.

q: Which of the following terms best describes Git?
exp: Git is a distributed version control system: every clone carries the full history and can commit, branch and merge offline. GitHub or GitLab are the hosting services built on top of it, which is what option (D) describes.

q:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

- P: In software engineering, defects that are discovered earlier are more expensive to fix.
- Q: A software design is said to be a good design if the components are strongly cohesive and weakly coupled.
exp: P is false — the cost of fixing a defect rises steeply the later it is found, so early defects are the cheap ones. Q states the classical design heuristic correctly: high cohesion within a module and low coupling between modules.
trick: High cohesion + low coupling is always the "good design" answer; any claim that early defects cost more is reversed.

q: Software products need adaptive maintenance for which of the following reasons?
opts: To rectify bugs observed while the system is in use
When the customers need the product to run on new platforms
To support new features that users want it to support
To overcome wear and tear caused by the repeated use of the software
exp: Adaptive maintenance responds to a change in the *environment* — a new OS, hardware, compiler or external interface. Fixing bugs is corrective maintenance and adding features is perfective maintenance; software does not physically wear out.
trick: Corrective = bugs, Adaptive = environment change, Perfective = new features/performance, Preventive = future-proofing.

q:
Which of the following are the primary objectives of risk monitoring in software project tracking?

- P: To assess whether predicted risks do, in fact, occur
- Q: To ensure that risk aversion steps defined for the risk are being properly applied
- R: To collect information that can be used for future risk analysis
opts: All of P, Q and R
exp: Risk monitoring in the RMMM plan has exactly these three aims: watch whether the predicted risks materialise, verify that the mitigation steps are actually being applied, and gather data that improves risk estimation on later projects.

q: The Model component in the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture is responsible for
opts: Translating between user interface actions/events and operations on the domain objects
exp: In MVC the Model holds the application state, the domain objects and the business rules. The View renders the user interface and the Controller maps user events onto model operations, which is exactly what option (D) describes.
trick: Model = data + business logic, View = presentation, Controller = the translator between them.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five generic framework activities of the software process?
exp: The five framework activities are Communication, Planning, Modeling, Construction and Deployment. Risk management is an **umbrella activity** — one of the eight that run across the whole life cycle alongside SQA, technical reviews, measurement, SCM, reusability management, tracking and control, and work product preparation.
trick: Any five-item list containing a management or assurance function is the umbrella list, not the framework list.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (model) | List-II (best-fitting situation) |
|---|---|
| (a) Waterfall | (i) requirements fuzzy on the customer's side |
| (b) Spiral | (ii) fixed, well-understood requirements and familiar technology |
| (c) Prototyping | (iii) reuse library available and a 60–90 day deadline |
| (d) RAD | (iv) large, expensive project with high technical risk |
exp: Waterfall assumes requirements are frozen and understood, which matches (ii). The spiral is the only classical model with explicit risk analysis on every circuit, so it owns (iv). Prototyping exists precisely because the customer cannot articulate what is wanted, which is (i). RAD's defining features are a 60–90 day timebox and heavy component reuse, which is (iii).
trick: Match on the single give-away word: risk → spiral, 60–90 days → RAD, cannot state requirements → prototyping.

q: In the V-model, the phase that is validated by integration testing is
exp: The V-model pairs each descending specification level with the ascending test level that validates it: requirements ↔ acceptance testing, system/architectural design ↔ system testing, component/high-level design ↔ integration testing, and module/detailed design ↔ unit testing. Integration testing therefore validates the component-level design, where the interfaces between modules were specified.
trick: Pair the V from the outside in; the outermost pair is always customer-facing (requirements ↔ acceptance).

q: Which statement about the spiral model is FALSE?
opts: It is risk-driven, with risk analysis performed on every circuit
The radial dimension represents cumulative cost and the angular dimension progress through a cycle
Each circuit produces a progressively more complete version of the system
It terminates when the software is delivered to the customer
exp: The spiral model is explicitly described as applying throughout the life of the software: after delivery, further circuits handle enhancement and maintenance, so it does **not** terminate at delivery. The other three statements are accurate descriptions of the model — risk-driven circuits, progressively more complete versions, and the radial/angular interpretation of the diagram.
trick: 'Terminates at delivery' is true of waterfall, false of the spiral. That contrast is the usual distractor.

q: A team must build control software that is embedded in a medical infusion pump, where an undetected fault could be fatal and the budget permits mathematical verification. The most appropriate process model is
exp: Safety-critical software whose correctness must be demonstrated rather than sampled is the defining application of the formal methods model, which specifies the system in Z, VDM or B and refines it by correctness-preserving transformations; Cleanroom software engineering is the best-known instance. RAD is explicitly unsuitable when technical risk is high, and neither incremental delivery nor prototyping provides a correctness argument.
trick: 'Mathematically verified' or 'safety-critical with adequate budget' always points at formal methods.

q:
Which of the following statements about process patterns are true?

A. A stage pattern describes a problem associated with one framework activity.
B. A phase pattern defines the sequence of framework activities for the whole project.
C. A task pattern has the widest scope of the three types.
D. The pattern template includes forces, initial context, problem, solution and resulting context.
exp: Task, stage and phase patterns increase in scope in that order, so a **task** pattern has the *narrowest* scope, not the widest — statement C is false. A stage pattern does correspond to a framework activity such as Communication, a phase pattern such as SpiralModel defines the activity sequence for the project, and Ambler's template does contain forces, initial context, problem, solution and resulting context.
trick: Task ⊂ Stage ⊂ Phase. Any option making task the broadest is wrong.

q: In the Unified Process, the phase in which an executable architectural baseline is established is
exp: Inception fixes the business case, rough scope and key use cases. Elaboration refines the use case model and delivers an executable architectural baseline — a running skeleton that demonstrates the architecture works. Construction then fills in the remaining components and Transition handles beta release, training and deployment.
trick: UP order is I-E-C-T; architecture is proven in E, not built in C.

q: Which CMMI maturity level is the first at which a single organisation-wide standard software process exists?
exp: Level 2 (Managed) brings discipline to individual projects — requirements management, planning, tracking, SCM and QA — but each project may work differently. Level 3 (Defined) is where the organisation tailors one standard process for all projects. Level 4 adds statistical control of process and quality, and Level 5 adds continuous measured improvement and defect prevention.
trick: If a question mentions statistical or quantitative control, the answer is 4; organisation-wide standard process is 3.

q: According to the Agile Manifesto, which of the following is correctly stated?
opts: Following a plan over responding to change
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
exp: The four values each put the agile preference on the left: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. Only "customer collaboration over contract negotiation" preserves that direction; the other three are stated backwards.
trick: Every value has the 'human, adaptive' side on the left. If an option puts the bureaucratic item first, it is inverted.

q: For a two-week Scrum sprint, which set of timeboxes is correct?
opts: Planning 4 h, Daily Scrum 7.5 min, Review 2 h, Retrospective 1.5 h
Planning 2 h, Daily Scrum 30 min, Review 1 h, Retrospective 1 h
Planning 8 h, Daily Scrum 15 min, Review 4 h, Retrospective 3 h
Planning 4 h, Daily Scrum 15 min, Review 2 h, Retrospective 1.5 h
exp: The one-month figures are Planning 8 h, Review 4 h and Retrospective 3 h, and these scale in proportion for a shorter sprint — halved for two weeks, giving 4 h, 2 h and 1.5 h. The Daily Scrum is the exception: it is fixed at 15 minutes for every sprint length because it re-plans the next 24 hours, and 24 hours does not scale.
trick: Everything halves for a half-length sprint except the Daily Scrum, which is always 15 minutes.

q: A Scrum team's last four sprints delivered 24, 30, 28 and 34 story points. The product backlog contains, in priority order, items of 8, 13, 5, 8, 3 and 13 points. Assuming the team plans to average velocity and takes items strictly in priority order, the number of sprints needed to complete the backlog is
exp: Average velocity $= (24+30+28+34)/4 = 116/4 = 29$ points per sprint. The backlog totals $8+13+5+8+3+13 = 50$ points. The number of sprints is $\lceil 50/29 \rceil = \lceil 1.72 \rceil = 2$.
trick: Sum the backlog, divide by average velocity, round up. Do not simulate the packing unless the question asks what fits in the next sprint.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (concept) | List-II (method) |
|---|---|
| (a) Spike solution | (i) DSDM |
| (b) MoSCoW | (ii) Lean |
| (c) Speculation, Collaboration, Learning | (iii) XP |
| (d) Defer commitment | (iv) ASD |
exp: A spike solution is XP's throwaway prototype for one hard design problem. MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't) is DSDM's prioritisation scheme. Speculation, Collaboration and Learning are the three phases of Highsmith's Adaptive Software Development. Defer commitment — decide as late as possible — is one of Lean's seven principles.
trick: Learn one unique keyword per method: spike → XP, MoSCoW → DSDM, Speculation → ASD, waste/defer → Lean, feature → FDD, colours → Crystal.

q: In Feature Driven Development, a feature is a client-valued function that should be implementable within
exp: FDD defines a feature using the template *action – result – object* and requires that any feature taking more than **two weeks** to build be decomposed into smaller features. That bound is what keeps FDD's plan-by-feature and build-by-feature activities tractable across large teams.
trick: FDD two weeks per feature, XP three weeks maximum per user story before splitting.

q:
Which of the following statements is/are true about Kanban?

A. It prescribes fixed-length iterations.
B. It limits work in progress explicitly per workflow stage.
C. It is a pull system rather than a push system.
D. It requires the roles of Product Owner and Scrum Master.
exp: Kanban's core practices are visualising the workflow, limiting work in progress, managing flow, making policies explicit, implementing feedback loops and improving collaboratively — so B and C are true. It deliberately prescribes **no** fixed iterations (A false) and **no** roles (D false); those belong to Scrum.
trick: Scrum limits time, Kanban limits work in progress. Any Kanban option mentioning sprints or Scrum roles is false.

q: In Extreme Programming, the correct order of events when implementing a user story is
opts: write the acceptance test, design the architecture, write the code, unit test
design the class, write the code, write the unit test, integrate
write the code, write the acceptance test, refactor, release
write the unit test, write the code, refactor, integrate continuously
exp: XP is test-first: the unit tests for a story are written before the code that satisfies them. Code is then written in pairs, refactored to keep the design simple, and integrated continuously — often several times a day. Acceptance tests are specified separately by the customer from the user stories and check externally visible behaviour.
trick: In any XP ordering question, 'write the unit test' comes first.

q: Which attribute is NOT characteristic of a WebApp as described in web engineering?
exp: WebApps are characterised by network intensiveness, concurrency, unpredictable load, performance and availability demands, being data- and content-driven, continuous evolution, immediacy of the delivery window, security exposure and the weight carried by aesthetics. Frozen requirements are the opposite of the immediacy and continuous-evolution attributes, which is precisely why incremental and agile processes dominate web engineering.
trick: The immediacy attribute (delivery in days or weeks) rules out any long linear front end, so 'frozen requirements' can never be a WebApp attribute.

q: Which agile principle states the primary measure of progress?
opts: Principle 1 — early and continuous delivery of valuable software
Principle 10 — simplicity, the art of maximising work not done
Principle 7 — working software is the primary measure of progress
Principle 12 — the team reflects at regular intervals
exp: Principle 7 states that working software is the primary measure of progress — that is, progress is not measured by documents produced, phases completed or percentage-complete reports. Principle 1 concerns delivery cadence, principle 10 concerns simplicity, and principle 12 is the basis of the Scrum retrospective.
trick: There are twelve principles; the three quoted most often are 7 (working software), 10 (simplicity) and 12 (reflection).

q: Which of the following is a functional requirement?
opts: The system shall respond to 95% of queries within 2 seconds
The system shall issue a refund receipt whenever a return is accepted
The system shall be available 99.9% of the time
The system shall be written in Java 17
exp: A functional requirement names a service the system provides. Issuing a refund receipt on an accepted return is such a service. Response time and availability are non-functional product requirements, and a mandated implementation language is a non-functional organisational (development) requirement.
trick: Ask 'what does it do' versus 'how well or under what constraint'. Performance, availability, security, portability and standards are always non-functional.

q: The correct order of the requirements engineering tasks is
opts: Inception, Elicitation, Elaboration, Specification, Negotiation, Validation
Inception, Elaboration, Elicitation, Specification, Validation, Negotiation
Elicitation, Inception, Negotiation, Elaboration, Validation, Specification
Inception, Elicitation, Elaboration, Negotiation, Specification, Validation
exp: Pressman's sequence is Inception, Elicitation, Elaboration, Negotiation, Specification, Validation, and then Requirements management running throughout. Negotiation precedes Specification because the conflicting demands are reconciled and prioritised **before** the agreed set is written down; writing first and negotiating afterwards would mean respecifying.
trick: Remember I-E-E-N-S-V-M, and note that Negotiation comes before Specification.

q: In a context diagram (level 0 DFD) for an order-processing system, the number of processes shown is
opts: determined by the number of use cases
exp: The context diagram represents the entire system as a single bubble, surrounded only by the external entities and the data flows between them and the system. Decomposition into several processes begins at level 1, and the levelling must be balanced: the level 1 diagram's net inputs and outputs must match those of the single level 0 bubble. Data stores also appear only from level 1 onwards.
trick: Level 0 means one bubble. Any option that makes the count depend on entities, stores or use cases is wrong.

q: Consider the requirement: *"The reporting module shall be efficient and easy to use."* Which pair of IEEE 830 qualities does it most directly violate?
exp: "Efficient" and "easy to use" carry no measurable criterion, so the requirement admits many interpretations (not unambiguous) and no finite, cost-effective process can decide whether the product satisfies it (not verifiable). Completeness, consistency, modifiability, ranking and traceability are properties of the document's organisation and coverage, and are not what this sentence breaks first.
trick: An adjective with no number attached almost always breaks unambiguous + verifiable together.

q: Which of the following statements about use cases is FALSE?
opts: A single use case may contain many scenarios
An actor represents a role, not a specific person
The <<extend>> relationship denotes behaviour that is always executed by the base use case
A secondary actor supports the system while a primary actor drives it
exp: The <<extend>> relationship denotes **conditional** behaviour added at a defined extension point, such as 'Print receipt' extending 'Withdraw cash'. The relationship that denotes always-executed, factored-out common behaviour is <<include>>. The other three statements are correct: actors are roles, a use case contains one primary and many alternative and exception scenarios, and primary versus secondary distinguishes the driving actor from the supporting one.
trick: include = always, extend = sometimes. Read for the words 'always' and 'optionally' in the stem.

q: In Quality Function Deployment, requirements so fundamental that the customer does not think to mention them — such as the system not crashing — are called
exp: QFD classifies requirements into three bands. **Normal** requirements are the objectives the customer states, and satisfaction rises with how well they are met. **Expected** requirements are implicit and fundamental; their absence causes dissatisfaction but their presence earns no credit. **Exciting** requirements go beyond expectation and delight when present. Domain requirements come from the application domain and are a separate classification.
trick: Unstated but assumed → expected; stated → normal; unasked-for delight → exciting.

q: Which section of an IEEE 830 SRS contains the detailed, individually verifiable requirements that developers and testers work from?
exp: Section 1 gives purpose, scope, definitions, references and overview. Section 2 is a non-binding overview for the reader — product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, constraints, assumptions and dependencies. Section 3, Specific requirements, holds the external interface, functional, performance, logical database, design constraint and software system attribute requirements in testable form.
trick: Numbered shall-statements live in section 3; narrative background lives in section 2.

q:
Arrange the following cohesion types in order of increasing cohesion:
(i) Communicational (ii) Logical (iii) Functional (iv) Temporal
exp: The full ladder from weakest to strongest is coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, functional. Restricting it to the four listed gives logical (2nd weakest), temporal (3rd), communicational (5th) and functional (strongest), i.e. (ii), (iv), (i), (iii).
trick: Drill 'Co-Lo-Te-Pro-Com-Se-Fun' and then just read off the subset in that order.

q:
Arrange the following coupling types in order of decreasing coupling (strongest first):
(i) Stamp (ii) Content (iii) Control (iv) Common
exp: The ladder from worst (tightest) to best (loosest) is content, common, external, control, stamp, data. Taking only the four listed and keeping that order gives content, common, control, stamp — option (ii), (iv), (iii), (i). Note that the question asks for **decreasing** coupling, which is the same direction as the worst-first ladder.
trick: Both ladders are conventionally written worst-first. Check the direction word ('increasing' vs 'decreasing') before matching.

q: A module `compute(record *r, int mode)` receives a complete employee record but reads only the `basic_pay` field, and the `mode` argument selects between two internal algorithms. The coupling between the caller and `compute` is best described as
exp: Passing a composite structure of which only one field is used is stamp coupling, because the callee is exposed to changes in fields it never reads. Passing a flag that selects which internal branch executes is control coupling. Both dependencies are present here, and when two forms coexist the design is characterised by the tighter of them — control coupling — but the question asks which are present, and the answer is both.
trick: A composite argument → stamp; a switch argument → control. A call can exhibit several coupling forms at once.

q: A module contains three statements: read the next transaction, validate it, and append a line to the audit log. The three share no data and no output feeds the next. Its cohesion is
exp: The three elements must run in that order but pass nothing between them, which is exactly procedural cohesion. Sequential cohesion would require the output of one element to be the input of the next. Communicational cohesion would require them all to operate on the same data, and functional cohesion would require them all to contribute to a single well-defined task.
trick: Order but no data flow → procedural. Order plus data flow → sequential.

q: Which statement about modularity is correct?
opts: Modularity and information hiding are the same concept
Interface cost is independent of the number of modules
Total development cost is minimised at an intermediate number of modules because interface cost rises with module count
Total development cost decreases monotonically as the number of modules increases
exp: Cost per module falls as modules get smaller, but the cost of integrating them rises with their number, so total cost is the sum of a falling and a rising curve and has a minimum — the region of minimum cost. Beyond it the design is overmodular. Information hiding is a distinct concept: it is the principle that each module conceals its design decisions, and it is the reason modular designs are maintainable.
trick: Draw the two curves. The exam answer to 'does more modularity always cost less?' is always no.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (architectural style) | List-II (description) |
|---|---|
| (a) Pipe and filter | (i) a central data store accessed by independent clients |
| (b) Repository | (ii) a hierarchy in which each level uses only the level below |
| (c) Layered | (iii) each component transforms an input stream into an output stream |
| (d) Call and return | (iv) a main program invokes subprograms and control returns to it |
exp: Pipe and filter is the data-flow style in which each filter transforms a stream — the compiler and Unix shell pattern. A repository is the data-centred style with a shared central store. Layered architecture restricts each layer to using the one beneath it, as in network stacks. Call and return is the main program/subprogram hierarchy with control returning to the caller.
trick: Identify the connector: a stream → pipe and filter, a shared store → repository, a strict hierarchy of use → layered.

q: In structured design, the mapping used when a single incoming data item triggers one of several mutually exclusive processing paths is
exp: Transaction mapping is applied when the data flow shows a transaction item that is evaluated and dispatched along one of several action paths; the resulting structure chart has a transaction centre acting as a dispatcher with one branch per path. Transform mapping is used for the pipeline shape with an incoming (afferent) flow, a central transform and an outgoing (efferent) flow. Factoring is the general act of decomposing a structure chart, not a mapping.
trick: Fan-out to mutually exclusive paths → transaction. A straight pipeline with a centre → transform.

q:
Consider the following statements about design concepts.

A. Abstraction and refinement are complementary: abstraction suppresses detail, refinement reveals it.
B. Information hiding limits the propagation of errors caused by a design change.
C. Functional independence is achieved by maximising both cohesion and coupling.
D. The scope of effect of a decision should lie within the scope of control of the module containing the decision.

Which are true?
exp: Statement C is false: functional independence requires **maximising cohesion and minimising coupling**, not maximising both. A is Wirth's standard formulation, B is precisely the benefit Parnas claimed for information hiding, and D is the classic structure-chart rule limiting the ripple of a decision.
trick: Any option claiming high coupling is desirable is wrong on sight.

q: Which of the following exhibits the WORST (tightest) form of coupling?
opts: Module A modifies a local variable inside module B by branching into the middle of B's code
Module A passes module B a boolean flag that selects B's processing algorithm
Module A passes module B a structure of which B uses two fields
Module A and module B both read and update a global configuration record
exp: Branching into another module's body and altering its local data is content coupling — the tightest and most pathological form, because a change to B's internals silently breaks A even when B's interface is unchanged. Common (global) coupling is the second worst, control coupling the third worst of those listed, and stamp coupling the loosest here.
trick: Content coupling is the only form where one module reaches *inside* another. Everything else goes through an interface of some kind.

q: McCall's quality factor *Interoperability* belongs to which category?
exp: Product Transition contains the three factors concerned with moving the software to a new setting: portability, reusability and interoperability. Product Operation holds correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity and usability; Product Revision holds maintainability, flexibility and testability. There is no category called Product Conformance.
trick: McCall splits 5-3-3. The two three-item groups are 'can it be changed' and 'can it be moved'; everything else is Operation.

q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

A. In ISO 9126, security is a sub-characteristic of Functionality.
B. In ISO 9126, testability is a sub-characteristic of Maintainability.
C. ISO 9126 defines eight quality characteristics.
D. ISO 25010 promotes Security to a top-level characteristic.
exp: ISO 9126 defines **six** characteristics — functionality, reliability, usability, efficiency, maintainability and portability — so C is false. Within them, security is a sub-characteristic of functionality (A true) and testability of maintainability (B true). The successor standard ISO 25010 raises the count to eight by promoting Security and adding Compatibility (D true).
trick: Six characteristics with security buried = 9126. Eight with Security standing alone = 25010. Any list with 'Correctness' is McCall.

q: A project plans to reuse 40 components. There is a 60% chance that 15 of them will be unavailable and must be built from scratch, each averaging 100 LOC at a cost of \$14 per LOC. The risk exposure is
exp: The cost if the risk materialises is $15 \times 100 \times 14 = \$21{,}000$. Risk exposure is $RE = P \times C = 0.60 \times 21{,}000 = \$12{,}600$. The distractor \$21,000 is the impact alone and \$8,400 is $0.4 \times 21{,}000$, the exposure of the complementary event.
trick: Compute the impact fully before multiplying by probability, and remember RE is money, never a fraction.

q: A server has an MTBF of 500 hours and an MTTR of 20 hours. Its availability is
exp: Since $\text{MTBF} = \text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}$, we get $\text{MTTF} = 500 - 20 = 480$ hours. Availability $= \text{MTTF}/\text{MTBF} = 480/500 = 0.96$, i.e. **96%**. The distractor 96.15% comes from computing $500/520$, which wrongly treats the given 500 as MTTF rather than MTBF.
trick: Read carefully whether the question gives MTBF or MTTF. Availability always divides MTTF by MTBF, so subtract MTTR first when MTBF is given.

q: A system has MTTF = 1000 hours and a constant failure rate. The probability that it operates without failure for a 100-hour mission is approximately
exp: With a constant failure rate, $\lambda = 1/\text{MTTF} = 0.001$ per hour and $R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-0.001 \times 100} = e^{-0.1} = 0.9048 \approx 0.905$. The value 0.90 is the linear approximation $1 - \lambda t$, which is close but not the exact exponential answer.
trick: $R(t) = e^{-t/\text{MTTF}}$. For small $t/\text{MTTF}$ the answer is just under $1 - t/\text{MTTF}$, which lets you eliminate options fast.

q: Which pairing of activity and category is correct?
opts: Conducting a code inspection — quality assurance
Defining the organisation's review procedure — quality assurance
Auditing whether the coding standard is being followed — quality control
Running the acceptance test suite — quality assurance
exp: Quality assurance is process-oriented and preventive: defining, auditing and training on processes and standards. Quality control is product-oriented and corrective: inspections, reviews and tests applied to a specific artefact. So defining a review procedure is assurance, while code inspection and acceptance testing are control, and an audit of standards compliance is assurance rather than control.
trick: If the activity acts on a *process*, it is assurance. If it acts on a specific *artefact*, it is control.

q: The three M's of an RMMM plan are
exp: RMMM stands for Risk Mitigation, Monitoring and Management. Mitigation acts now to reduce a risk's probability or impact; monitoring watches indicators to see whether the risk is becoming more likely and whether mitigation is being applied; management executes the contingency plan once the risk trigger fires.
trick: Mitigate before, monitor during, manage after. The trigger is the event that switches monitoring into management.

q: An application has 32 external inputs, 60 external outputs, 24 external inquiries, 8 internal logical files and 2 external interface files, all of average complexity. The unadjusted function point count is
trick: Memorise the average column 4-5-4-10-7; most questions use average complexity throughout.

q: For the application above, the fourteen general system characteristics sum to 35. The adjusted function point count is
exp: $\text{VAF} = 0.65 + 0.01 \times 35 = 0.65 + 0.35 = 1.00$, so FP $= 618 \times 1.00 = 618$ — the adjustment is exactly neutral. A sum of 35 across the fourteen characteristics is the break-even point at which the adjusted and unadjusted counts coincide.
trick: $\sum F_i = 35$ always gives VAF = 1.00. Spotting that saves the whole calculation.

q: The value adjustment factor in the function point method can vary between
exp: $\text{VAF} = 0.65 + 0.01\sum F_i$ where each of the fourteen characteristics is rated 0 to 5, so $\sum F_i$ ranges from 0 to 70. That gives VAF from $0.65 + 0 = 0.65$ to $0.65 + 0.70 = 1.35$ — the adjustment can move the count by at most ±35%.
trick: 14 characteristics × 5 max = 70, and 0.01 × 70 = 0.35. The band is always 0.65 to 1.35.

q: A 100 KLOC project is developed in organic mode. Using basic COCOMO ($a=2.4$, $b=1.05$, $c=2.5$, $d=0.38$), the estimated effort and development time are approximately
exp: $E = 2.4 \times 100^{1.05} = 2.4 \times 125.89 = 302.1$ person-months. Then $D = 2.5 \times 302.1^{0.38} = 2.5 \times 8.76 = 21.9$ months. The distractor 13.8 is the average team size $N = E/D = 302.1/21.9 = 13.8$ people, not a duration.
trick: $100^{1.05} = 10^{2.1} = 125.9$ — powers of ten make organic-mode arithmetic easy.

q: A 32 KLOC embedded-mode project is estimated with basic COCOMO. The effort is
exp: Embedded mode uses $a = 3.6$ and $b = 1.20$, so $E = 3.6 \times 32^{1.2}$. Because $32 = 2^5$, $32^{1.2} = 2^{6} = 64$ exactly, giving $E = 3.6 \times 64 = 230.4$ PM. The other options are organic basic (91.33), organic intermediate with EAF 1 (121.76) and semi-detached basic (145.51) for the same size.
trick: Check whether KLOC is a power of two — the embedded exponent 1.20 then gives an exact answer with no logarithms.

q: Which set of intermediate COCOMO multipliers $a$ is correct for organic, semi-detached and embedded modes respectively?
exp: Basic COCOMO multipliers *increase* with difficulty (2.4, 3.0, 3.6) because the whole penalty for a hard project is carried by the multiplier. Intermediate COCOMO multipliers *decrease* (3.2, 3.0, 2.8) because the penalty is now carried by the fifteen cost drivers in the effort adjustment factor instead. Semi-detached is 3.0 in both, which anchors the pattern.
trick: If the question mentions an EAF or cost drivers it is intermediate (3.2/3.0/2.8); if it gives only size and mode it is basic (2.4/3.0/3.6).

q: In COCOMO II's post-architecture model, the exponent $E$ in $\text{PM} = A \times \text{Size}^{E} \times \prod \text{EM}_i$ is computed as
opts: a fixed constant chosen by the development mode
exp: COCOMO II's main conceptual advance over COCOMO 81 is that the exponent is **estimated** rather than fixed by a mode: $E = B + 0.01\sum SF_j$ with $B = 0.91$ and five scale factors PREC, FLEX, RESL, TEAM and PMAT. The seventeen effort multipliers enter as a product, not in the exponent, and $0.65 + 0.01\sum F_i$ is the function point VAF.
trick: Scale factors go in the exponent; effort multipliers go in the product. A = 2.94, B = 0.91.

q: Using Putnam's software equation, if the development time for a project is halved while the size and technology constant remain unchanged, the required effort is multiplied by
exp: Putnam's equation $L = C_k K^{1/3} t_d^{4/3}$ rearranges to $K = L^3/(C_k^3 t_d^4)$, so effort varies as the inverse **fourth** power of development time. Halving $t_d$ therefore multiplies $K$ by $2^4 = 16$. This is the fourth-power trade-off law, the quantitative form of the warning against schedule compression.
trick: $K_1/K_2 = (t_2/t_1)^4$ — size and $C_k$ cancel, so ratio questions need no absolute numbers.

q: A project is estimated at 250 person-months. Applying the 40-20-40 rule, the effort allocated to coding is
exp: The 40-20-40 rule allocates 40% to analysis and design, **20% to coding** and 40% to testing and debugging. So coding takes $0.20 \times 250 = 50$ person-months, while analysis/design and testing take 100 person-months each.
trick: Coding is the smallest of the three. The distractor is the reading '40-40-20' with coding second.

q: At a project review, BCWS = 120 PM, BCWP = 100 PM and ACWP = 110 PM. Which statement is correct?
opts: The project is ahead of schedule and under budget
The project is ahead of schedule but over budget
The project is behind schedule but under budget
The project is behind schedule and over budget
exp: $\text{SPI} = \text{BCWP}/\text{BCWS} = 100/120 = 0.83 < 1$, so less work has been completed than was scheduled — behind schedule. $\text{CPI} = \text{BCWP}/\text{ACWP} = 100/110 = 0.91 < 1$, so more was spent than the completed work was budgeted for — over budget. Equivalently $\text{SV} = -20$ PM and $\text{CV} = -10$ PM.
trick: BCWP is the numerator of both indices. An index below 1 or a negative variance is always bad news.

q: For the program fragment `a = b + c; d = a * b;`, treating `=`, `+`, `*` and `;` as operators, Halstead's program volume $V$ is
exp: Distinct operators $n_1 = 4$ (`=`, `+`, `*`, `;`) with total occurrences $N_1 = 2+1+1+2 = 6$. Distinct operands $n_2 = 4$ (`a`, `b`, `c`, `d`) with $N_2 = 2+2+1+1 = 6$. So vocabulary $n = 8$, length $N = 12$, and $V = N\log_2 n = 12 \times 3 = 36$.
trick: $V = N\log_2 n$ uses the *total* counts for $N$ and the *distinct* counts for $n$ — mixing them is the usual error.

q: Top-down integration testing requires ___ , while bottom-up integration testing requires ___ .
exp: A stub replaces a module that the module under test **calls**, so top-down integration — which starts at the main control module before the lower levels exist — needs stubs. A driver replaces the module that **calls** the module under test, so bottom-up integration — which starts at the leaves before any caller exists — needs drivers. Sandwich integration needs both.
trick: Top-down, stubs down. Bottom-up, drivers up.

exp: Count the predicate nodes: the loop condition `i < n` is one; the compound condition `a[i] % 2 == 0 && a[i] > 0` splits into **two** predicate nodes because each simple condition is an independent decision; and `c == 0` is the fourth. So $V(G) = 4 + 1 = 5$.
trick: A compound condition joined by && or || contributes one predicate node per simple condition, not one per `if`.

q: A program's flow graph has 17 edges, 13 nodes and is a single connected component. The number of independent paths in its basis set is
exp: $V(G) = E - N + 2P = 17 - 13 + 2(1) = 6$, and the basis set contains exactly $V(G)$ independent paths. Cross-checks: the graph must contain 5 predicate nodes ($5 + 1 = 6$) and, drawn in the plane, 6 regions counting the unbounded one.
trick: Compute $V(G)$ two ways whenever you can — predicate nodes + 1 must equal $E - N + 2$.

q: Which of the following statements about cyclomatic complexity is FALSE?
opts: It equals the number of regions in the planar flow graph, counting the unbounded region
It gives an upper bound on the number of tests needed to ensure every statement is executed at least once
Every path in the basis set is guaranteed to be executable with some input
It equals the number of predicate nodes plus one
exp: The basis set is derived from the graph's topology, not from the program's semantics, so some basis paths may be infeasible — for example a path that skips a loop whose guard is always true on the first iteration. Testers substitute realisable paths that cover the same previously untraversed edges; the value of $V(G)$ does not change. The other three statements are all correct definitions or properties.
trick: 'Every basis path is executable' is the standard false option. The count is topological, not semantic.

q: A module has three independent input variables. The number of test cases generated by worst-case boundary value analysis is
exp: Worst-case BVA takes all combinations of the five values min, min⁺, nominal, max⁻ and max for every variable, giving $5^n = 5^3 = 125$ test cases. The distractors are normal BVA ($4n+1 = 13$), robust BVA ($6n+1 = 19$) and robust worst-case BVA ($7^n = 343$).
trick: Linear forms ($4n+1$, $6n+1$) hold all but one variable at nominal; exponential forms ($5^n$, $7^n$) take all combinations. 'Robust' adds the two out-of-range values.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (a) Error | (i) an observed deviation of delivered behaviour from required behaviour |
| (b) Fault | (ii) a human action that produces an incorrect result |
| (c) Failure | (iii) an incorrect step, process or data definition in the artefact |
| (d) Debugging | (iv) the activity of locating and removing the cause of a known failure |
exp: The causal chain is error → fault → failure. A human makes an **error** (ii), which leaves a **fault** in the artefact (iii), which on execution may produce a **failure** (i). Debugging (iv) follows testing and removes the fault once a failure has revealed it. A fault that is never executed produces no failure at all.
trick: Error is in the head, fault is in the code, failure is in the behaviour.

q: Which statement correctly describes beta testing?
opts: It is conducted at end-user sites in a live environment with the developer generally absent
It is conducted by the development team before the software leaves the organisation
It precedes alpha testing in the validation sequence
It is conducted at the developer's site with the developer recording problems
exp: Beta testing is a live application of the software at one or more customer sites, with the developer normally not present; users report problems at intervals. Alpha testing comes first and takes place at the developer's site in a controlled environment with the developer observing. Testing by the development team itself is neither alpha nor beta.
trick: Alpha = at home, developer watching. Beta = out in the field, developer absent. Alpha always precedes beta.

q: Which of the following statements about coverage criteria is TRUE?
opts: Full condition coverage always implies full decision (branch) coverage
Full statement coverage always implies full branch coverage
Full branch coverage always implies full statement coverage
Full path coverage is always achievable in practice
exp: Executing every branch necessarily executes every statement, so branch coverage subsumes statement coverage. The converse fails — a single test can execute all statements of an `if` without an `else` while never taking the false branch. Condition coverage does not imply decision coverage either: for `if (a || b)`, the tests (T,F) and (F,T) cover both values of both conditions yet take the true branch twice. Path coverage is generally infeasible because loops give unbounded path counts.
trick: Branch ⊃ statement is safe; condition ⊃ branch is not, which is why MC/DC exists.

q: In testing a simple loop that can execute at most $n$ times, the recommended set of tests includes passes of
exp: Loop testing prescribes skipping the loop entirely, one pass, two passes, $m$ passes with $m < n$, and the boundary set $n-1$, $n$ and $n+1$ — the $n+1$ case verifying that the loop cannot over-run. Testing every value from 0 to $n$ is exhaustive and unnecessary, and the reduced sets omit the boundaries where faults cluster.
trick: The seven-case loop pattern always includes 0, 1, 2 and the triple $n-1$, $n$, $n+1$.

q:
Which of the following statements is/are true?

A. Verification is primarily a static activity and validation primarily a dynamic one.
B. A successful test, in Myers's sense, is one that uncovers an as-yet-undiscovered error.
C. Regression testing means re-executing the complete test suite after every change.
D. Stress testing deliberately demands abnormal quantity, frequency or volume of resources.
exp: Statement C is false: regression testing selects a representative sample of existing tests plus tests focused on the functions likely to be affected and on the components actually changed — re-running everything is usually infeasible. A, B and D are all standard: verification uses reviews and inspections, Myers defines a successful test as one that finds a new error, and stress testing pushes resource demand far beyond normal.
trick: Any option describing regression testing as 'complete retesting' is wrong — the whole technique is about selection.

q: A field accepts an integer in the range 1 to 100. Applying equivalence partitioning, the minimum number of test cases needed to cover all equivalence classes for this field is
exp: A range $a..b$ yields one valid class ($1 \le x \le 100$) and two invalid classes ($x < 1$ and $x > 100$) — three classes in total, so three test cases, one representative from each. Six would be the boundary value count (testing $0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101$), which is a different technique.
trick: Range → 1 valid + 2 invalid classes. Specific value → 1 valid + 2 invalid. Set of values → 1 valid per member + 1 invalid. Boolean → 1 valid + 1 invalid.

q: A software configuration item that has been formally reviewed and agreed upon, and thereafter can be changed only through formal change control procedures, is called
exp: That is the IEEE definition of a baseline, in three parts: formally reviewed and agreed, serving as the basis for further development, and changeable only through formal change control. A build produces an executable from a configuration, a variant is a functionally equivalent instance for a different environment, and a release is a version distributed to customers.
trick: The three-part IEEE wording is quoted almost verbatim in exam stems — reviewed, basis for further work, formal change control only.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a revision from a variant?
opts: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
A revision replaces its predecessor; a variant co-exists with functionally equivalent siblings
A revision co-exists with its predecessor; a variant replaces it
A revision changes functionality; a variant fixes defects
exp: A revision is created to correct faults in or improve on a previous version and is intended to **supersede** it, forming a sequence 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 along an evolution path. A variant is functionally equivalent but built for a different environment or configuration — the same release for Windows and for Linux — and the variants **co-exist** as branches rather than replacing one another.
trick: Replace = revision, co-exist = variant. That one test settles every version-control terminology item.

q:
Arrange the change control steps in the correct order:
(i) Engineering change order generated (ii) Change request submitted (iii) Change control authority decides (iv) Change report produced (v) Object checked out of the project database
exp: The request comes first and is evaluated for technical merit, side effects, impact on other configuration objects and cost; that evaluation is written up as a change report. The change control authority then decides on status and priority, and only if it approves is an engineering change order generated. The object is checked out after the ECO exists, changed, reviewed and audited, then checked in.
trick: Evaluate → report → decide → ECO → check out. Nothing is checked out before the CCA has approved.

q: Which maintenance category accounts for the largest share of maintenance effort, according to the classical Lientz and Swanson survey?
exp: The survey shares are approximately perfective 50%, adaptive 25%, corrective 21% and preventive 4%. Maintenance is therefore dominated by **enhancement** at user request, not by bug-fixing. Adaptive maintenance responds to a changed environment, and preventive maintenance (re-engineering) improves future maintainability before a problem appears.
trick: Candidates guess corrective. The survey says perfective — remember 'maintenance is mostly making it do more'.

q: Which statement correctly relates reverse engineering, restructuring and re-engineering?
opts: Reverse engineering lowers the level of abstraction; restructuring raises it
Re-engineering is performed before the system is first delivered
Restructuring preserves the abstraction level; reverse engineering raises it; re-engineering combines reverse and forward engineering
Reverse engineering and restructuring are synonyms; re-engineering is unrelated
exp: Reverse engineering analyses code to produce a representation at a **higher** level of abstraction — design recovery — and changes nothing. Restructuring changes the form of code or data while preserving behaviour and the **same** abstraction level. Re-engineering is the full cycle: reverse engineering to recover the design, followed by forward engineering to rebuild the system in an improved form.
trick: Draw the abstraction arrow: up = reverse, down = forward, sideways = restructuring, up-then-down = re-engineering.

q: Building a component to a reusable standard costs 1.6 times the cost $C$ of building it for a single use, and each subsequent reuse costs $0.2C$ in qualification, adaptation and integration. The smallest number of applications at which building for reuse becomes cheaper than building afresh each time is
exp: Cost of building afresh $n$ times is $nC$; cost of building once for reuse and using it $n$ times is $1.6C + 0.2Cn$. Setting them equal gives $1.6 = 0.8n$, so $n = 2$ exactly — at $n = 2$ the two are equal ($2.0C$ each) and reuse is not yet *cheaper*. The first $n$ at which reuse strictly wins is therefore $n = 3$, where reuse costs $2.2C$ against $3.0C$.
trick: Break-even is $n = p/(1-r)$ with build premium $p$ and per-reuse cost $r$. If it comes out an exact integer, the strictly cheaper point is the next integer up.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six activities of the software re-engineering process model?
exp: The re-engineering cycle consists of inventory analysis, document restructuring, reverse engineering, code restructuring, data restructuring and forward engineering. Requirements elicitation is a requirements-engineering task, not part of the re-engineering model, which works from an existing legacy system rather than from stakeholders.
trick: The six activities all act on an existing system. Anything that involves gathering new requirements from scratch is outside the model.
